327.name: encode_cross_crate
327.docs:
Whether this builtin attribute is encoded cross crate.
This means it can be used cross crate.

250.name: WarnFollowing
250.docs:
Duplicates after the first attribute will be an unused_attribute warning.

This is usually used for "word" attributes, where they are used as a
boolean marker, like `#[used]`. It is not necessarily wrong that there
are duplicates, but the others should probably be removed.

325.name: BUILTIN_ATTRIBUTES
325.docs: Attributes that have a special meaning to rustc or rustdoc.

752.name: UNSTABLE_LANG_FEATURES
752.docs:
Unstable language features that are being implemented or being
considered for acceptance (stabilization) or removal.

398.name: enabled_lang_features
398.docs: `#![feature]` attrs for language features, for error reporting.

44.name: into
44.docs: Calls `U::from(self)`. That is, this conversion is whatever the implementation of [From]<T> for U chooses to do.

169.name: Gated
169.docs: A gated attribute which requires a feature gate to be enabled.

294.name: encode_cross_crate
294.docs:
Whether this attribute is encode cross crate.

If so, it is encoded in the crate metadata.
Otherwise, it can only be used in the local crate.

369.name: unstable
369.docs: List of the unstable feature gates.

167.name: check
167.docs: Check function to be called during the `PostExpansionVisitor` pass.

165.name: feature
165.docs: The feature gate, for example `#![feature(rustc_attrs)]` for rustc_* attributes.

13.name: Normal
13.docs:
Normal, builtin attribute that is consumed
by the compiler before the unused_attribute check

642.name: incomplete
642.docs:
Some features are known to be incomplete and using them is likely to have
unanticipated results, such as compiler crashes. We warn the user about these
to alert them.

792.name: from_environment
792.docs:
This takes into account `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP`.

If `krate` is [`Some`], then setting `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=krate` will enable the nightly
features. Otherwise, only `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1` will work.

363.name: REMOVED_LANG_FEATURES
363.docs: Formerly unstable features that have now been removed.

788.name: Allow
788.docs: Allow use of unstable features, as on nightly.

209.name: AttributeTemplate
209.docs:
A template that the attribute input must match.
Only top-level shape (`#[attr]` vs `#[attr(...)]` vs `#[attr = ...]`) is considered now.

409.name: enabled_features_iter_stable_order
409.docs: Returns a iterator of enabled features in stable order.

207.name: name_value_str
207.docs:
If `Some`, the attribute is allowed to be a name/value pair where the
value is a string, like `#[must_use = "reason"]`.

5.name: Features
5.docs:
A set of features to be used by later passes.

There are two ways to check if a language feature `foo` is enabled:
- Directly with the `foo` method, e.g. `if tcx.features().foo() { ... }`.
- With the `enabled` method, e.g. `if tcx.features.enabled(sym::foo) { ... }`.

The former is preferred. `enabled` should only be used when the feature symbol is not a
constant, e.g. a parameter, or when the feature is a library feature.

684.name: stable_since
684.docs: If the lang feature is stable, the version number when it was stabilized.

205.name: list
205.docs: If `Some`, the attribute is allowed to take a list of items like `#[allow(..)]`.

255.name: FutureWarnPreceding
255.docs:
Duplicates preceding the last instance of the attribute will be a
warning, with a note that this will be an error in the future.

This is the same as `FutureWarnFollowing`, except the last attribute is
the one that is "used". Ideally these can eventually migrate to
`ErrorPreceding`.

3.name: accepted
3.docs: List of the accepted feature gates.

884.name: template
884.docs:
A convenience macro for constructing attribute templates.
E.g., `template!(Word, List: "description")` means that the attribute
supports forms `#[attr]` and `#[attr(description)]`.

682.name: gate_name
682.docs: Name of the feature gate guarding the language feature.

253.name: ErrorPreceding
253.docs:
Duplicates preceding the last instance of the attribute will be an error.

This is the same as `ErrorFollowing`, except the last attribute is the
one that is "used". This is typically used in cases like codegen
attributes which usually only honor the last attribute.

1.name: ACCEPTED_LANG_FEATURES
1.docs: Formerly unstable features that have now been accepted (stabilized).

755.name: since
755.docs:
For unstable features: the version the feature was added in.
For accepted features: the version the feature got stabilized in.
For removed features we are inconsistent; sometimes this is the
version it got added, sometimes the version it got removed.

251.name: WarnFollowingWordOnly
251.docs:
Same as `WarnFollowing`, but only issues warnings for word-style attributes.

This is only for special cases, for example multiple `#[macro_use]` can
be warned, but multiple `#[macro_use(...)]` should not because the list
form has different meaning from the word form.

401.name: EnabledLibFeature
401.docs: Information about an enabled library feature.

124.name: Normal
124.docs: Normal attribute that does not need `#[unsafe(...)]`

753.name: INCOMPATIBLE_FEATURES
753.docs:
Some features are not allowed to be used together at the same time, if
the two are present, produce an error.

249.name: DuplicatesOk
249.docs:
Duplicates of this attribute are allowed.

This should only be used with attributes where duplicates have semantic
meaning, or some kind of "additive" behavior. For example, `#[warn(..)]`
can be specified multiple times, and it combines all the entries. Or use
this if there is validation done elsewhere.

399.name: EnabledLangFeature
399.docs: Information about an enabled language feature.

170.name: Ungated
170.docs: Ungated attribute, can be used on all release channels

168.name: notes
168.docs: Notes to be displayed when an attempt is made to use the attribute without its feature gate.

166.name: message
166.docs: The error message displayed when an attempt is made to use the attribute without its feature gate.

14.name: CrateLevel
14.docs: Builtin attribute that is only allowed at the crate level

643.name: internal
643.docs:
Some features are internal to the compiler and standard library and should not
be used in normal projects. We warn the user about these to alert them.

793.name: from_environment_value
793.docs:
Avoid unsafe `std::env::set_var()` by allowing tests to inject
`std::env::var("RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP")` with the `env_var_rustc_bootstrap`
arg.

364.name: removed
364.docs: List of the removed feature gates.

10.name: find_gated_cfg
10.docs: Find a gated cfg determined by the `pred`icate which is given the cfg's name.

789.name: Cheat
789.docs:
Errors are bypassed for bootstrapping. This is required any time
during the build that feature-related lints are set to warn or above
because the build turns on warnings-as-errors and uses lots of unstable
features. As a result, this is always required for building Rust itself.

787.name: Disallow
787.docs: Disallow use of unstable features, as on beta/stable channels.

208.name: docs
208.docs: A link to the document for this attribute.

206.name: one_of
206.docs:
If non-empty, the attribute is allowed to take a list containing exactly
one of the listed words, like `#[coverage(off)]`.

256.name: AttributeDuplicates
256.docs: How to handle multiple duplicate attributes on the same item.

885.name: rustc_feature
885.docs:
# Feature gates

This crate declares the set of past and present unstable features in the compiler.
Feature gate checking itself is done in `rustc_ast_passes/src/feature_gate.rs`
at the moment.

Features are enabled in programs via the crate-level attributes of
`#![feature(...)]` with a comma-separated list of features.

For the purpose of future feature-tracking, once a feature gate is added,
even if it is stabilized or removed, *do not remove it*. Instead, move the
symbol to the `accepted` or `removed` modules respectively.

406.name: enabled_lang_features
406.docs:
Returns a list of [`EnabledLangFeature`] with info about:

- Feature gate name.
- The span of the `#[feature]` attribute.
- For stable language features, version info for when it was stabilized.

204.name: word
204.docs: If `true`, the attribute is allowed to be a bare word like `#[test]`.

254.name: FutureWarnFollowing
254.docs:
Duplicates after the first attribute will be an unused_attribute warning
with a note that this will be an error in the future.

This should be used for attributes that should be `ErrorFollowing`, but
because older versions of rustc silently accepted (and ignored) the
attributes, this is used to transition.

404.name: set_enabled_lang_feature
404.docs:
`since` should be set for stable features that are nevertheless enabled with a `#[feature]`
attribute, indicating since when they are stable.

127.name: Unsafe
127.docs:
Unsafe attribute that requires safety obligations to be discharged.

An error is emitted when `#[unsafe(...)]` is omitted, except when the attribute's edition
is less than the one stored in `unsafe_since`. This handles attributes that were safe in
earlier editions, but become unsafe in later ones.

252.name: ErrorFollowing
252.docs:
Duplicates after the first attribute will be an error.

This should be used where duplicates would be ignored, but carry extra
meaning that could cause confusion. For example, `#[stable(since="1.0")]
#[stable(since="2.0")]`, which version should be used for `stable`?
